title: India Hosts BRICS Summit as Iran War Divides the Bloc's Newest Members
excerpt: Leaders from 11 BRICS nations gather in New Delhi on September 12-13, with the U.S.-led war on Iran - pitting Iran against fellow member UAE - testing the bloc's ability to issue a joint declaration.
body:
• India hosts the BRICS Leaders' Summit in New Delhi on September 12–13, its first time chairing the expanded 11-member bloc.
  • The U.S.- and Israel-led war on Iran, now past its sixth month, pits two BRICS members — Iran and the UAE — on opposing sides, with the UAE suspending all trade and financial transactions with Tehran in August.
  • The conflict has virtually shut the Strait of Hormuz and pushed crude above $100 a barrel, raising the stakes for energy-importing members including India.
  • Xi Jinping's first visit to India in seven years, plus scheduled Modi–Xi and Modi–Putin bilaterals, puts China and Russia alongside host India at the center of efforts to hold the bloc together.

Summit Opens Under the Shadow of War

India hosts the BRICS Leaders' Summit this weekend, seeking to lift the bloc's global profile even as the U.S.-led war on Iran splits its membership, with Tehran and Abu Dhabi on opposing sides of the conflict, according to Reuters. The September 12–13 summit in New Delhi comes more than six months after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran, a BRICS member since 2024.

https://x.com/Outlookindia/status/2098011248038158474

The conflict has virtually shut the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's key oil-trade choke points, pushing crude above $100 a barrel. The UAE — hit by Iranian missiles since the war began — announced an indefinite embargo on August 19, accusing Iranian forces of firing two ballistic missiles at its territory, and suspended all trade and financial transactions with Iran. Tehran denied the allegation, calling it a "false flag operation" by Israel and the United States, the Hindu BusinessLine reported.

Context & Background

BRICS began as Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining later, and has expanded over the past two years to 11 members with the addition of Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the UAE and Indonesia. Saudi Arabia's role remains ambiguous: it has not accepted full membership but participates with lower-level delegations, and Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud will attend the Delhi meeting.

The Iran–UAE rift has already derailed consensus once this year. At the BRICS foreign ministers' meeting in New Delhi in May, members failed to issue a joint statement over differences between Iran and the UAE, and India released a chair's statement instead. At the Trade Ministers' meeting in Jaipur earlier this month, objections to one paragraph Tehran wanted included blocked a joint communique; the meeting adopted a chair's statement with four annexes instead.

A hopeful precedent: at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek earlier this month, Modi, Xi, Putin and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian signed a joint declaration condemning the U.S.-Israeli campaign against Iran — language acceptable to members with differing positions. On August 31, Modi met Pezeshkian on the sidelines, their first meeting since the war broke out.

Impact & Analysis

The key test, foreign policy experts told Reuters, is finding language on the Middle East crisis acceptable to both Abu Dhabi and Tehran, clearing the way for a joint declaration. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday the differences had a "negative impact" on drafting one, but hoped leaders would find acceptable phrasing.

"Some of (BRICS') new members, Iran and the UAE, Egypt and Ethiopia are embroiled in tensions and don't agree much. This is bad news for an entity that operates based on consensus."

— Michael Kugelman, senior fellow, Atlantic Council

Former Indian diplomat Rajiv Bhatia said the SCO outcome — achieved without the UAE at the table — has raised hopes that "an acceptable formulation" is possible for BRICS too. Experts also said Trump's protectionist tariff policies have given members reasons to come together, potentially enabling two-way or three-way leader meetings on the margins.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, the summit is more than spectacle. Millions of Indian workers live in the UAE and across the Gulf, directly exposed to the escalation. Crude above $100 a barrel feeds India's import bill and inflation — and the purchasing power of remittances. And how New Delhi balances Moscow, Beijing and U.S. pressure over Russian oil is watched closely by diaspora investors and professionals whose businesses straddle all three.

What's Next

Attention now shifts to the bilaterals. A likely Modi–Xi meeting would be their third since last year's agreement to ease military tensions along the disputed Himalayan border. Peskov confirmed Putin will hold talks with Modi on Friday, with trade and economic cooperation high on the agenda — Russia remains one of India's largest energy suppliers.

By Sunday evening, the outcome will be measured in documents: a joint declaration would signal the expanded bloc can still find consensus despite war within its ranks; another chair's statement would confirm that expansion has made agreement harder, not easier.
